208: How Unity’s D28 IAP ROAS optimizer prevents D7 cannibalization
209: The question remains that if both campaign types bid on impressions in the same inventory, won’t they compete against each other and drive up costs?
210: Unity's analysis of D28 converters reveals that only 38%* of users who convert with in-app purchases by D28 spend in the first week. In other words, roughly two-thirds of high-value D28 spenders showed no early IAP conversion signals whatsoever.
211: These aren’t players who nearly converted on D7 but needed a few more days. They’re a different player cohort with different motivations, engagement patterns, and conversion triggers.
212: This is where Unity Vector's support is vital. Traditional optimization models can only see what happens after a user installs: Did they convert? How much did they spend? Unity Vector enables Unity IAP ROAS optimizers to see something more.
213: Because Unity powers both game creation and user growth, Unity Vector has unique visibility into player behavior and patterns.
214: Unity Vector combines holistic player and game intelligence to understand why certain players match with certain games, and when they're likely to convert. It uses both attributed data and unattributed data, like cross-game behavioral patterns and aggregate cohort insights, to distinguish between these player types at the moment of bid decision.
215: The future of ROAS optimization with Unity Vector
216: When UA efficiency increasingly plays a large role in which games succeed and which fail, leaving only 38% of IAP converters addressed isn't viable. And without the early converters of D7 campaigns, optimizers have less signals and businesses have less to invest in their late-game campaigns.
217: Both are necessary. And with Unity Vector powering both optimization windows, these Unity Ads campaign types can deliver better results as the model learns from Unity's place at the intersection of game creation and growth.
218: The architectural decision to optimize for holistic player and game intelligence means Unity Vector's optimization capabilities improve alongside games as they evolve and player behaviors shift - allowing Unity Vector to provide later LTV predictions as the market demands increasingly longer optimization windows. Ultimately, this ensures Unity is able to help creators build games that players love to play, and turn those games into profitable, sustainable businesses.
219: Ready to expand your optimization strategy?

223: Internal Unity data, D7 IAP/D28 IAP Comparative Analysis, April 2024 - February 2025

14: As the controller of your Developer Data, it’s your responsibility to respect end-user consent as is applicable to your business. Generally, this means you must present your users with appropriate opportunities to affirm or reject the various ways in which you intend to use their personal data.
15: 
16: To help you fulfill this responsibility, Unity has introduced the End-User Consent Mode: a developer-friendly way to manage user consent dynamically across supported Unity services.
17: 
18: Consent Mode allows end users to express their desired intent when making a particular consent decision. As a result, Unity products and services will be able to understand end-user consent relative to a particular use case – as opposed to service level Collect/Don’t Collect APIs that may unnecessarily suppress the value of the service to developers.
19: 
20: Consent Mode is fully integrated with the Developer Data framework and consolidates end-user consent management for all Unity products and services that operate using Developer Data. It works by allowing you to declare default consent states for your users and to maintain changes to their consent states in near real time along the following dimensions:
21: 
22: * `analytics_intent` 
23:   Controls whether Developer Data may be used in analytics and analytics-derived use cases that involve user-level identifiers.
24: 
25: * `ads_intent` 
26:   Controls whether Developer Data may be used in personalized advertising use cases and the collection of ads-specific device identifiers.
27: 
28: Each signal supports two values:
29: 
30: * `granted`: Unity will proceed with data collection and will use the data from the consenting user in accordance with the customer’s Developer Data usage settings.
31: * `denied`: Unity will suppress purpose-specific identifier collection for the unconsenting user, and may, where applicable, limit the collection of data events which are specific to applicable intent. Unity will act in accordance with the customer’s Developer Data usage settings, however, personal data from unconsented users will be filtered-out as indicated by the user.
32: 
33: Consent Mode is a core component of Unity’s Developer Data framework and applies specifically to your use of Developer Data pursuant to framework controls. Obtaining the proper consent from your end users is often critical. Consent Mode helps you align with privacy regulations and user expectations while maintaining transparency and control over how Developer Data is used across Unity products and services.
34: 
35: If no default end-user consent is configured via Consent Mode, Unity assumes that you’ve chosen to manage those states using another method, such as a developer-controlled implementation or service-specific consent APIs. In the event no end-user consent state is knowable or available, Unity interprets the lack of signal as if the set values were the following:
36: 
37: * `analytics_intent = granted`
38: * `ads_intent = denied`

20: We spend a lot of time talking to advertisers about measurement. Not because measurement is the most exciting topic in performance marketing, but because it's where confusion lives. And confusion, more than budget, more than creative, is usually what holds a brand back from getting the most out of a channel.
21: The conversations tend to go one of two ways. Either an advertiser comes to us saying AppLovin looks strong in-platform, but their third-party tool doesn't see it. Or they come in saying their MMM is actually attributing more to AppLovin than the platform itself reports. Both end up in the same place. The disagreement between those numbers is not telling you who is right. It is telling you what each model was built to see.
22: Stop waiting for one number to tell the whole story
23: Here is a simple way to think about it. A customer sees an AppLovin ad while playing a mobile game on a Tuesday afternoon. They don't click. Three days later, they search for the brand on Google, land on the site, and buy. On Friday, their roommate, reached by the same campaign, buys on Amazon without ever touching the DTC site.
24: Today, AppLovin's in-platform report sees neither of those conversions. Click-based attribution requires a click, and none happened. Your MTA tool picks up the Google search and gives it credit, maybe with a partial assist somewhere upstream. Your MMM may pick up that AppLovin spend correlates with a broader lift in demand, including the Amazon sale. Your post-purchase survey captures neither customer because they were never prompted. An incrementality test, run well, is the only instrument that would tell you with statistical confidence how many of those conversions genuinely would not have happened without the campaign.
25: None of those answers is wrong. They are just not measuring the same thing.
26: The advertiser who uses all of them to triangulate is in a much better position than the one waiting for a single source of truth that doesn't exist.
27: Half of what AppLovin drives never shows up in the dashboard
28: Fospha, which measures AppLovin across a growing cohort of ecommerce brands, has found that last-click and MTA models are significantly underreporting AppLovin's contribution, because the channel operates at a discovery layer those tools aren't built to see.
29: Source:
30: Fospha's AppLovin Playbook
31: Prescient's MMM benchmark series adds another layer:
32: Across our AppLovin cohort, roughly 50% of modeled value comes through halo, higher than Meta (~42%) or Google (~40%), and nearly half of that halo lands on Amazon. For brands with a heavy Amazon presence, the story is even stronger: halo climbs to ~60% of modeled value. The hypothesis makes sense: AppLovin is reaching high-intent users in mobile environments who convert later on Amazon, the channel they already trust for purchasing.
33: Will Holtz, Prescient COO & CFO
34: Both partners are pointing at the same thing. AppLovin's in-platform reporting is conservative, and its contribution is showing up well beyond what last-click captures.
35: AppLovin's impact is growing faster than its own reporting shows
36: We have now worked through a growing body of incrementality tests on AppLovin over the past 17 months since the first incrementality test came in. A few things stand out.
37: Tests have gotten better built over time. Advertisers have come to understand the mechanics now - what a holdout is doing, why test duration and geo balance matter, what a clean result actually requires. And because we review most designs before they launch, fewer tests go live underpowered or with a geo split that was never going to balance. None of that shows up as a single headline number. It shows up as results a brand can feel reasonably confident in and act on, instead of results we have to hedge.
38: The platform picture is also changing in ways that matter here. The incremental factor we observe, a brand's iROAS measured by a geo holdout experiment relative to its AppLovin in-platform reported ROAS, has more than doubled over the past year. In-platform reporting currently captures click-through attribution only and that gap between what the platform reports and what a controlled experiment reveals has been consistent with the third-party signals above: a meaningful share of what AppLovin drives isn't visible in its own reporting.
39: Not ready to test yet is not a reason to stop optimizing
40: The brands with the most consistent results understand that an incrementality test is a moment-in-time experiment with real constraints. Holdout size, budget level, test duration, geo composition, campaign stability - all of these interact.
41: A few of these we hold firm on: campaigns need to be out of the learning phase and delivering steadily before a test starts, holdouts are typically sized at 20-50% of the geo footprint, and we design every test to a minimum of 90% statistical power.

40: Media & creative
41: Media and creative feel like the easiest functions to integrate inside of a brand. Media needs assets to run in channels; creative needs performance data to produce better concepts. Yet at too many brands, these teams operate in parallel without integrated workflows.
42: This disconnect is especially costly on algorithmically driven platforms like AppLovin, where little to no manual targeting exists by design. Our models match the right user to the right ad relative to the conversion event the brand wants to achieve.
43: Media buyers still want to ensure they’re reaching new and diverse audiences and that their reach is expanding over time. On AppLovin Ads, creative is the primary lever to do this.
44: We encourage creative teams on our platform to think like media buyers. They control the targeting more than the media team does. Want to reach women? Make ads for women. Want to reach millennials? Make content that resonates with them. The model will find the right audience for whatever the creative team produces.
45: Breaking down the walls
46: None of these silos are unique to AppLovin. They exist across every marketing channel. But because AppLovin Ads is algorithmically driven and performance-based, the cost of these organizational gaps shows up faster and more visibly in the data.

10: # Post-install event data
11: 
12: > Pass post-install event data from your app to Unity Ads through an MMP to optimize user acquisition campaigns based on real user engagement, such as sessions, purchases, ad revenue, and level completions.
13: 
14: Unity Ads User Acquisition campaigns that are optimized for acquiring particular kinds of users, such as [Retention](/grow/acquire/campaigns/retention/retention-campaigns.md), [Return on Ad Spend](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/return-on-ad-spend-campaigns.md) (ROAS), and [Event](/grow/acquire/campaigns/event/event-campaigns.md) campaigns, require information about how users engage with your app after installing it. Post-install event data informs Unity's models to more accurately show ads to your campaign's target audience.
15: 
16: When you integrate with an MMP, you can enable your preferred partner to pass post-install event data to Unity. Each type of optimized campaign requires at least one type of post-install event data. However, you can pass data from all event types to any of your campaigns. The recommended best practice is to pass data for all post-install events because the additional data can improve your campaign performance.
17: 
18: Integrated partners can pass the following types of post-install event data:
19: 
20: | Post-install event | Description                                                           | Related campaigns                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
21: | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
22: | Session            | Users open your app                                                   | [Retention](/grow/acquire/campaigns/retention/retention-campaigns.md)                                                                                                                                                              |
23: | Purchase           | Purchases users make in your app                                      | * [In-app Purchase (IAP) ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/purchase/in-app-purchase.md)
24: * [Hybrid ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/hybrid/hybrid.md)
25: * [Payer](/grow/acquire/campaigns/event/intro-to-event-campaigns.md#payer) |
26: | Ad revenue         | Revenue from ads that your users watch in your app                    | - [Ad Revenue ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/ad-revenue/ad-revenue.md)
27: - [Hybrid ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/hybrid/hybrid.md)                                                                                          |
28: | Level Complete     | A specific milestone or completion event your users reach in your app | [Level Complete](/grow/acquire/campaigns/event/intro-to-event-campaigns.md#level-complete)                                                                                                                                         |

20: This topic explains how budget settings dictate how much marketing spend your user acquisition campaigns could consume.
21: 
22: > **Important:**
23: >
24: > Campaign budget limits are estimates. Because actual spend depends on many factors including campaign performance, Unity does not guarantee that you will be invoiced according to the budget limit amount.
25: 
26: ## Organization budgets##organiza
27: 
28: The overall marketing budget your organization has available to spend with Unity's ad platform is called an Organization budget. If the organization budget reaches zero, all activity with the organization's ad campaigns will pause until there is an available organization budget to spend from.
29: 
30: Your active ad campaigns consume your organization budget. To limit how much of your organization budget an individual campaign can spend, you can set two kinds of campaign-level budgets:
31: 
32: * **Campaign budget**: the overall budget for an individual campaign
33: * **Daily budget**: the target spending for a single day in an individual campaign
34: 
35: Both the campaign budget and the daily budget are optional campaign settings. If you leave these budget settings empty, the campaign will spend an unlimited amount until the organization budget is consumed or the campaign ends.
36: 
37: > **Note:**
38: >
39: > Use the [Reporting dashboard](/grow/acquire/reporting/dashboard/reporting-dashboard.md) or the [Advertiser Statistics API](/grow/acquire/reporting/api-reports.md) to understand how your organization consumes its budget.
40: 
41: ### Budget remaining##budget
42: 
43: You can view the balance of your organization budget in the bottom of the Unity Ads User Acquisition dashboard secondary navigation menu. You can also select **Budget remaining** > **Add funds** to make payments to your organization budget. For more information, refer to the [Budgets and payments](/grow/acquire/budgets.md) documentation.
44: 
45: > **Note:**
46: >
47: > If you have set up post payments with a client partner, the **Budget remaining** section will display **Credit line in use** instead of a balance amount. Refer to the [Post payments](/grow/acquire/budgets/payments/introduction.md#post) documentation for more information.
48: 
49: ## Campaign budgets##campaign
50: 
51: Campaign budgets determine how much of your organization budget can be consumed by an individual campaign. Campaign budgets are optional; if you do not set a campaign budget, your campaign will spend an unlimited amount of your overall organization budget.
52: 
53: ## Daily budget##daily
54: 
55: Use Daily budgets to set a target for how much of the campaign budget you would like the campaign to spend each day. Think of the daily budget as an average daily spend of your campaign budget. The Unity User Acquisition system will use the target budget to throttle your campaign as you reach the limit.
56: 
57: However, successful campaigns with low budgets might occasionally overspend the daily budget. Daily budgets reset at midnight, UTC. When you set a daily budget, you can choose between a campaign-level budget or country-level budgets. Country-level budgets can be individual or grouped:
58: 
59: * **Campaign-level daily budget**: A single daily limit that applies across all countries.
60: * **Per-country daily budget**: Individual daily limits for each targeted country.
61: * **Multi-country daily budget**: A shared daily budget pooled across a group of countries, with Unity's algorithm automatically distributing spend within the group based on performance.

63: ### Multi-country daily budgets
64: 
65: Multi-country daily budgets allow you to share a campaign's daily spending limit across multiple grouped budgets. Each budget group can contain multiple countries. You define groups of countries and set one shared budget per group. Unity's optimization system then distributes spend across the countries in each group in real time, prioritizing where bids win and conversions happen.
66: 
67: > **Tip:**

69: > Multi-country budgets work simultaneously with per-country daily budgets in the same campaign.
70:

For guidance on when to use them and how to structure your groups, refer to [Budget best practices](/grow/acquire/budgets/best-practices.md). For setup instructions, refer to [Set daily budgets](/grow/acquire/budgets/set-daily-budget.md).

73: ### Daily Cap status
74: 
75: The Daily Cap is a set of campaign statuses that notify you when a live campaign has already spent its daily budget. Campaigns with the Daily Capped and Geo Capped statuses are not currently spending, even though they are set as live.
76: 
77: > **Note:**
78: >
79: > Daily Cap statuses are only visible for live campaigns. For more information, review the documentation on how to [set campaigns live](/grow/acquire/campaigns/set-campaigns-live.md).
80: 
81: The following table details the Daily Cap statuses and their corresponding [daily budgets](/grow/acquire/budgets/set-daily-budget.md):
82: 
83: | **Status**   | **Daily budget** | **Description**                                                                                                                          |
84: | ------------ | ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
85: | Daily Capped | All countries    | The campaign is live but is unable to deliver ads because it has met its daily budget.                                                   |
86: | Geo Capped   | Per country      | The campaign is live but is unable to deliver ads (or is partially delivering ads) because one or more country has met its daily budget. |

14: ## Optimize budgets
15: 
16: Automated bidding is one option for controlling your daily campaign spend. Automated bidding dynamically adjusts your bids throughout the day to optimize how your budget is used. You can use both CPM and CPI billing with Automated bidding.
17: 
18: When you use cost per install (CPI) billing without Automated bidding, successful campaigns will occasionally spend their campaign budget too quickly when they have several successful days in one week. Automated bidding can help you maintain budget limits on a weekly basis. If your campaign overspends one day, Automated bidding adjusts your budget for the next day to compensate. This ensures your campaign stays within budget on a weekly basis.
19: 
20: When you set your daily budget with Automated bidding, aim for one-seventh of the amount you want your campaign to spend in a week. Use this calculation for both CPI-billed and CPM-billed campaigns.
21: 
22: Automated bidding also optimizes your bids so your budget is used more efficiently. By adjusting your bids based on campaign performance, Automated bidding maximizes the number of installs your campaign can achieve in a day.
23: 
24: ### Optimize budgets with ROAS campaigns
25: 
26: ROAS (return on ad spend) campaigns also benefit from Automated bidding. When you run a ROAS campaign, with CPI billing, the campaign automatically uses Automated bidding. This bidding strategy helps improve campaign performance for campaigns that are constrained by their daily cap. By optimizing how your bids are placed, using CPI billing in these campaigns can increase your observed return on ad spend (ROAS).
27: 
28: For more information about [Automated bids](/grow/acquire/bids.md), refer to the Bids documentation.
29: 
30: > **Important:**
31: >
32: > Changing your budget might have an impact on how accurately the daily budget can be respected on a weekly basis. If you change your budget mid-campaign, it will take approximately seven days for the system to accurately respect the new budget on a weekly basis.

35: 
36: When you start adding budgets to your campaign, Unity offers recommendations for your minimum campaign budget and minimum daily budget. These recommendations are based on the billing type, the number of creatives assigned, and the countries the campaign is targeting.

79: ### Set daily budgets based on weekly targets
80: 
81: Unity's budget management operates on a 7-day rolling window rather than enforcing hard daily limits. Daily spend varies slightly from day to day within that window. If your campaign overspends on one day, spend will be lower on subsequent days to compensate, and vice versa. Over a full week, the average daily spend will meet your goal.
82:

13: Auction dynamics
14: The MAX In-App Bidding Exchange is a first-price, fair and transparent, unified first-price auction in which the highest bidder wins.
15: All SDK in-app bidders and DSPs have equal access to each ad impression opportunity.
16: They receive full notification coverage with enhanced macros.
17: The MAX In-App Bidding Exchange collects bids for individual impression opportunities from SDK-based demand partners and DSPs.
18: It does this via the OpenRTB 2.5 protocol.
19: To integrate with MAX, a bidder must comply with the OpenRTB 2.5 API.
20: To read the MAX in-app bidding spec for SDK-based in-app bidders, see
21: the AppLovin oRTB specification page
22: MAX ad serving flow
23: The user launches the app.
24: MAX initializes all eligible SDKs.
25: The publisher requests an ad.
26: For SDK bidders, MAX collects bid tokens from initialized SDKs.
27: MAX SDK makes an ad request to MAX ad server.
28: MAX auction server requests bids from eligible SDK bidder endpoints and DSPs in AppLovin Exchange.
29: It passes identity tokens in the bid request to SDK bidders.
30: DSPs and SDK bidders return real-time bids in the maximum timeout threshold (
31: tmax
32: ).
33: MAX auction server merges these with the non-bidding demand sources in the publisher waterfall.
34: MAX auction server resolves the auction based on the highest CPM value.
35: MAX sends loss notifications to bidders that lose the auction due to error or invalid bid (e.g. below the floor, missing bid value, zero as bid price).
36: If the winner is a DSP, MAX notifies the DSP and the AppLovin SDK loads and shows the ad.
37: If the winner is an SDK bidder, MAX notifies the winning demand partner’s SDK so that it can load and show the ad.
38: If the load succeeds, MAX sends a win notification to the bidder.
39: If the load does not succeed, MAX sends a loss notification to the bidder.
40: After the ad renders, MAX calls the winner’s billing URL.

20: ### Overview
21: 
22: A publishing app submits an ad request to Unity's exchange, where DSPs can submit a bid for the impression. If the bid wins the auction, Unity pre-caches the ad and only renders it when the user views the ad. At this point, an impression and all other trackers are counted.
23: 
24: 1. Unity receives an ad request from a mobile device.
25: 2. Unity makes an HTTP POST [request](/grow/programmatic/unity-exchange/bid-requests.md) to all bidding partner endpoints.
26: 3. For waterfall auctions, TMAX is configurable by the DSP seat, up to 1000ms. For bidding auctions, TMAX is configured by the mediation platform; 50ms is deducted from Unity's processing time. In both scenarios, the DSP's time to respond is communicated in the bid request.
27: 4. Unity's Exchange runs a first-price auction based on valid bidder responses.
28: 5. Upon completing the auction, Unity retrieves the winning bid's HTML and impression trackers to the client for pre-caching.
29: 6. When the player experiences the ad, Unity pings the winning bidder's `nURL` to notify the DSP of the impression.

208: How Unity’s D28 IAP ROAS optimizer prevents D7 cannibalization
209: The question remains that if both campaign types bid on impressions in the same inventory, won’t they compete against each other and drive up costs?
210: Unity's analysis of D28 converters reveals that only 38%* of users who convert with in-app purchases by D28 spend in the first week. In other words, roughly two-thirds of high-value D28 spenders showed no early IAP conversion signals whatsoever.
211: These aren’t players who nearly converted on D7 but needed a few more days. They’re a different player cohort with different motivations, engagement patterns, and conversion triggers.
212: This is where Unity Vector's support is vital. Traditional optimization models can only see what happens after a user installs: Did they convert? How much did they spend? Unity Vector enables Unity IAP ROAS optimizers to see something more.
213: Because Unity powers both game creation and user growth, Unity Vector has unique visibility into player behavior and patterns.
214: Unity Vector combines holistic player and game intelligence to understand why certain players match with certain games, and when they're likely to convert. It uses both attributed data and unattributed data, like cross-game behavioral patterns and aggregate cohort insights, to distinguish between these player types at the moment of bid decision.
215: The future of ROAS optimization with Unity Vector
216: When UA efficiency increasingly plays a large role in which games succeed and which fail, leaving only 38% of IAP converters addressed isn't viable. And without the early converters of D7 campaigns, optimizers have less signals and businesses have less to invest in their late-game campaigns.
217: Both are necessary. And with Unity Vector powering both optimization windows, these Unity Ads campaign types can deliver better results as the model learns from Unity's place at the intersection of game creation and growth.
218: The architectural decision to optimize for holistic player and game intelligence means Unity Vector's optimization capabilities improve alongside games as they evolve and player behaviors shift - allowing Unity Vector to provide later LTV predictions as the market demands increasingly longer optimization windows. Ultimately, this ensures Unity is able to help creators build games that players love to play, and turn those games into profitable, sustainable businesses.
219: Ready to expand your optimization strategy?
220: Get started

223: Internal Unity data, D7 IAP/D28 IAP Comparative Analysis, April 2024 - February 2025

36: ## Learning phase best practices
37: 
38: The following best practices are specific to the [Learning phase](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/intro-to-roas-campaigns.md#learning-phase) of your ROAS campaign.
39: 
40: ### Collect unattributed postbacks from the Unity SDK
41: 
42: To accelerate your campaign's learning phase, use the Unity SDK to collect additional SDK data and ensure that you send Unity the corresponding post-install event’s [unattributed](/grow/acquire/partner-integration/attribution/introduction.md#attribution-types)  postbacks for at least two weeks before you create your new ROAS campaign. This data won’t be counted as part of the learning threshold, but helps to train the machine learning models that enable optimization. When you supply unattributed postbacks and SDK data before campaign launch, it can improve initial optimization predictions and help shorten the Learning phase.
43: 
44: ### Avoid setup changes during the Learning phase
45: 
46: While your campaign is in the Learning phase, avoid making changes to your campaigns settings, such as budgets or targeting parameters. Performance fluctuations are normal during this phase. Making changes during the Learning phase can disrupt the machine learning process and extend the Learning phase. After your campaign reaches **Live** status, you can optimize your settings for better performance.
47: 
48: ### Adjust ROAS goal if install volume is too low
49: 
50: While you should generally avoid setup changes during the Learning phase, you might need to adjust your ROAS goal if your campaign can't reach the [required install threshold](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/intro-to-roas-campaigns.md#learning-phase-thresholds). If your campaign has been in the Learning phase for an extended period without meeting the install requirement, lower your ROAS goal. This allows the system to place higher CPI bids and acquire more users, helping your campaign exit the Learning phase.
51: 
52: ### Focus on United States and Tier 1 countries during the Learning phase
53: 
54: During the learning phase, the recommended best practice is to launch with US or multiple top performing Tier 1 or Tier 2 countries. Tier 3 countries typically have lower user density and monetization rates, which can make it difficult to collect sufficient data during the Learning phase. This is especially true for IAP and Hybrid campaigns, which require payer data.
55: 
56: ## MMP integration best practices
57: 
58: The following best practices are specific to your preferred Mobile Measurement Partner (MMP) [integration](/grow/acquire/partner-integration.md) setup.
59: 
60: ### Send install data from all sources
61: 
62: When you share install data with Unity, ensure that you include data from your entire user base, including attributed, unattributed, and organic installs. Refer to the [Introduction to Attribution](/grow/acquire/partner-integration/attribution/introduction.md#attribution-types) for definitions of each attribution type.
63: 
64: ### Share both values and revenue for Purchase and Ad Revenue events
65: 
66: When you share Purchase or Ad revenue event data with Unity, share both values and revenue for each event. Sharing this complete data improves Unity's User Acquisition models and can improve campaign performance.
67: 
68: ### Set postback windows to lifetime if applicable
69: 
70: If your MMP supports lifetime postback windows, always set the window to lifetime. Otherwise, set your postback window to the maximum length. Setting your postback window to lifetime allows your campaign to learn from your app's entire install history and can improve campaign performance.

20: Consent Mode is fully integrated with the Developer Data framework and consolidates end-user consent management for all Unity products and services that operate using Developer Data. It works by allowing you to declare default consent states for your users and to maintain changes to their consent states in near real time along the following dimensions:
21: 
22: * `analytics_intent` 
23:   Controls whether Developer Data may be used in analytics and analytics-derived use cases that involve user-level identifiers.
24: 
25: * `ads_intent` 
26:   Controls whether Developer Data may be used in personalized advertising use cases and the collection of ads-specific device identifiers.
27: 
28: Each signal supports two values:
29: 
30: * `granted`: Unity will proceed with data collection and will use the data from the consenting user in accordance with the customer’s Developer Data usage settings.
31: * `denied`: Unity will suppress purpose-specific identifier collection for the unconsenting user, and may, where applicable, limit the collection of data events which are specific to applicable intent. Unity will act in accordance with the customer’s Developer Data usage settings, however, personal data from unconsented users will be filtered-out as indicated by the user.
32: 
33: Consent Mode is a core component of Unity’s Developer Data framework and applies specifically to your use of Developer Data pursuant to framework controls. Obtaining the proper consent from your end users is often critical. Consent Mode helps you align with privacy regulations and user expectations while maintaining transparency and control over how Developer Data is used across Unity products and services.
34: 
35: If no default end-user consent is configured via Consent Mode, Unity assumes that you’ve chosen to manage those states using another method, such as a developer-controlled implementation or service-specific consent APIs. In the event no end-user consent state is knowable or available, Unity interprets the lack of signal as if the set values were the following:
36: 
37: * `analytics_intent = granted`
38: * `ads_intent = denied`

15: AppLovin Ad Review runs only on impressions MAX mediates, and only after a publisher turns it on in the MAX dashboard. There is no scenario where we take another network's ad output and train our models on it. Even so, we are removing the user-level detail entirely. 20: Direct integration: MAX to you
21: There are three ways you can get user-level revenue data:
22: User revenue API:
23: Use this API to retrieve user-level revenue data on a daily basis.
24: You can retrieve this data in two forms: aggregated for a particular user or with one row per impression.
25: Data is available eight hours after UTC day end.
26: Learn more on
27: the user revenue API documentation page
28: .
29: Client-side:
30: You can access impression-level user revenue data on the client side in real-time.
31: You can find integration instructions for
32: Android
33: and
34: iOS
35: in this documentation.
36: Server-to-server:
37: You can also access real-time revenue data on the server side.
38: To do this, provide an impression postback that tracks impression-level user ad revenue data.
39: Contact your account team or
40: the support team
41: to enable this feature.
42: This feature, and the macros that the impression postback supports, are described in
43: the “Server-to-server impression revenue API” section
44: of this page.
45: MMP integration: MAX to MMP
46: MAX has analytics partners who can help you access your data in a single dashboard.
47: You can work with any of AppLovin’s supported partners to access impression-level ad revenue or aggregated ad revenue data.
48: These supported partners include
49: Adjust
50: ,
51: GameAnalytics
52: ,
53: AppsFlyer
54: , and
55: Singular
56: .
57: Refer to the documentation pages maintained by those partners for more information about their capabilities.
58: Server-to-server impression revenue API
59: Contact your account team or
60: the support team
61: to enable this feature.
62: AppLovin’s servers can send postbacks to an external endpoint whenever they record a MAX impression.
63: You define which endpoint receives these requests.
64: The postbacks are in the form of HTTP or HTTPS
65: GET
66: requests.
67: AppLovin makes these postbacks soon after the impression, but they may be delayed by a few minutes.
68: You can use an impression timestamp macro to reconcile any delay between the impression and the postback times.
69: The postback request times-out if five seconds pass without a response from your endpoint.
70: There are no retries for postback requests.
71: Example
72: https://myimpressionserver.com/impression?idfa={IDFA}&user_id={USER_ID}&event={EVENT_ID}&token={EVENT_TOKEN}
73: Available macros
74: You can incorporate any of the macros in the following table into your postback URL.
75: The example URL above incorporates the
76: {IDFA}
77: ,
78: {USER_ID}
79: ,
80: {EVENT_ID}
81: , and
82: {EVENT_TOKEN}
83: macros.
84: AppLovin’s servers replace these macro names with accurate values when the servers make the request to your endpoint.
85: Name
86: Description
87: {AD_UNIT_ID}
88: MAX ad unit ID (16 hex characters)
89: Example:
90: 9ad0816ac071552a
91: {AD_UNIT_NAME}
92: Ad unit name (URL-encoded)
93: Example:
94: My%20App%20Banners
95: {AD_UNIT_TEST_NAME}
96: Name of the ad unit test, URL-encoded
97: Example:
98: Control
99: {ALL_REVENUE}
100: Estimated revenue, including FB Bidding estimates
101: Examples:
102: 0.0121
103: ,
104: 5.74466e-05
105: {CC}
106: Two-letter country code of the user
107: Example:
108: gb
109: {CUSTOM_DATA}
110: Custom data passed in from the integration (URL-encoded). AppLovin recommends that you keep the size of the string under 8192 characters. You must not include ampersand (
111: &
112: ) characters in the custom data if you include this macro.
113: Example:
114: my%20custom%20data
115: {DEVICE_TYPE}
116: User’s device type.
117: Example:
118: Tablet
119: {EVENT_ID}
120: Unique event ID, 36-character UUID
121: Example:
122: a7c3e1b2-4f59-4d8a-9c21-8e6b0f3a1d47
123: {EVENT_TOKEN}

12: > Pass post-install event data from your app to Unity Ads through an MMP to optimize user acquisition campaigns based on real user engagement, such as sessions, purchases, ad revenue, and level completions.
13: 
14: Unity Ads User Acquisition campaigns that are optimized for acquiring particular kinds of users, such as [Retention](/grow/acquire/campaigns/retention/retention-campaigns.md), [Return on Ad Spend](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/return-on-ad-spend-campaigns.md) (ROAS), and [Event](/grow/acquire/campaigns/event/event-campaigns.md) campaigns, require information about how users engage with your app after installing it. Post-install event data informs Unity's models to more accurately show ads to your campaign's target audience.
15: 
16: When you integrate with an MMP, you can enable your preferred partner to pass post-install event data to Unity. Each type of optimized campaign requires at least one type of post-install event data. However, you can pass data from all event types to any of your campaigns. The recommended best practice is to pass data for all post-install events because the additional data can improve your campaign performance.
17: 
18: Integrated partners can pass the following types of post-install event data:
19: 
20: | Post-install event | Description                                                           | Related campaigns                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
21: | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
22: | Session            | Users open your app                                                   | [Retention](/grow/acquire/campaigns/retention/retention-campaigns.md)                                                                                                                                                              |
23: | Purchase           | Purchases users make in your app                                      | * [In-app Purchase (IAP) ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/purchase/in-app-purchase.md)
24: * [Hybrid ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/hybrid/hybrid.md)
25: * [Payer](/grow/acquire/campaigns/event/intro-to-event-campaigns.md#payer) |
26: | Ad revenue         | Revenue from ads that your users watch in your app                    | - [Ad Revenue ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/ad-revenue/ad-revenue.md)
27: - [Hybrid ROAS](/grow/acquire/campaigns/roas/hybrid/hybrid.md)                                                                                          |
28: | Level Complete     | A specific milestone or completion event your users reach in your app | [Level Complete](/grow/acquire/campaigns/event/intro-to-event-campaigns.md#level-complete)                                                                                                                                         |
29: 
30: > **Note:**
31: >
32: > To run an [Event optimization](/grow/acquire/campaigns/event/event-campaigns.md.md) campaign (Retention, Payer, or Level Complete), you must use one of the following MMPs:
33: >
34: > * Adjust
35: > * AppsFlyer
36: > * Singular
37: 
38: ## Supported post-install events
39: 
40: Most MMPs support passing post-install event data, usually through server postback URLs. To run optimized ad campaigns, use your preferred MMP's dashboard to set up post-install event passing.
41: 
42: > **Note:**
43: >
44: > Sharing some event data types might require additional subscriptions with your preferred MMP. Refer to the individual [Partner integration](/grow/acquire/partner-integration.md) guides in this documentation for information about your partner's requirements.
45: 
46: Refer to the following tables for which event types each of these common integrated partners support:
47: 
48: | **MMP**   | **Session** | **Purchase** | **Ad revenue** | **Level Complete** |
49: | --------- | ----------- | ------------ | -------------- | ------------------ |
50: | AppsFlyer | Yes         | Yes          | Yes            | Yes                |
51: | Adjust    | Yes         | Yes          | Yes            | Yes                |
52: | Singular  | Yes         | Yes          | Yes            | Yes                |
53: | Tenjin    | Yes         | Yes          | Yes            | No                 |
54: | Branch    | Yes         | Yes          | No             | No                 |
55: | Kochava   | Yes         | Yes          | No             | No                 |
56: 
57: > **Important:**
58: >
59: > Ensure that you carefully follow your attribution partner's integration instructions. Incorrect integrations will result in loss of event data because your servers can't retroactively send data from events.

5: Attribute ad revenue to complete the LTV (lifetime value) performance view.
6: Ad revenue attribution
7: Ads display in the app on banners, offer walls, interstitials, etc., and create ad revenue.
8: Ad revenue, combined with in-app purchases and subscription revenue, provides you with the complete LTV picture of the user. By matching user LTV to the media spend campaign, you can determine ROI and analyze it on the platform.
9: Attributed ad revenue data
10: :
11: Is acquired from the mediation platforms or ad monetization networks via server APIs or by embedded reporting SDK in the app (including iOS 14).
12: Is attributed to the media source that originally brought the user, for example:
13: User sees an ad from Network A and downloads your app.
14: Ad displays inside the app.
15: Ad revenue is attributed to Network A (responsible for user acquisition), regardless of who published the ad.
16: Reporting granularity depends on the monetization network integration and ad revenue attribution type.
17: Integration types for ad revenue attribution
18: Data accuracy and freshness depend on the ad revenue attribution integration type, as shown in the following table.
19: Note
20: : SDK integration types require developer assistance to implement. S2S integration types require you to have the correct network credentials.
21: Ad revenue attribution integration type
22: Description
23: Aggregate level
24: via S2S API
25: AppsFlyer receives daily revenue, broken down by geo.
26: The effective revenue per action (eRPA) is derived by dividing the revenue by the number of instances of a trigger event.
27: The trigger events are either app open or specific in-app events set in the app.
28: If you're using a mediation platform, make sure to disable ad revenue integrations for monetization partners mediated via the platform before enabling the ad revenue integration with the platform. Failure to do so results in duplicate data.
29: Data is not available in raw data reports and cannot be shared with ad networks via postbacks or UA signals.
30: Device-level
31: via S2S API
32: The mediation platform or monetization network reports the revenue by user at the device level. Not all networks support device-level granularity.
33: This revenue is attributed to the media source that brought the user. Meaning AppsFlyer ad revenue attribution adheres to the attribution rules found in the platform, including retargeting attribution rules.
34: If you're using a mediation platform, make sure to disable ad revenue integrations for monetization partners mediated via the platform before enabling the ad revenue integration with the platform. Failure to do so results in duplicate data.
35: Device-level via S2S API includes 100% of ad revenue and offers the highest data accuracy among ad revenue integration types.
36: Data is available in raw data reports and can be shared with ad networks only via
37: UA signals.

172: When an app uses two
173: mediation platforms
174: with API integration types (aggregate-level or device-level), both associated with the same
175: monetization network
176: , partial duplication of ad revenue data may occur. In such cases, each mediation platform reports all the ad revenue generated by its associated monetization network, regardless of whether that revenue was generated while being mediated by only one of the platforms.
177: To help avoid partial duplication of revenue data when two mediation platforms cross-reference each other
178: :
179: If available, use impression-level integrations via SDK. Impression-level data reported this way isn't deduplicated. The SDK reports each impression once, so there's no overlap to remove.
180: For integrations
181: via API

184: Settings

186: Revenue Settings
187: >

191: General Settings
192: , check the box
193: Deduplicate ad revenue when two mediation partners cross-reference each other
194: .
195: Note
196: : Don't check the box if the 2 mediation platforms mediate different ad formats. For example, when platform 1 shows Banner and Interstitial, and platform 2 shows AppOpen and Native ads.

204: Aggregate granularity using app open or in-app events
205: Aggregate granularity for ad revenue works as follows:
206: The integrated network reports total daily revenue, broken down by geo.
207: AppsFlyer derives the effective revenue per action (eRPA) by dividing the ad revenue with the number of instances of a trigger event.
208: AppsFlyer creates a _monetized event that includes the total eRPA for each attributed device. For example, ad_matched_monetized.

sources.excerpt:
23: LTV vs. Activity
24: There are two methods for analyzing user event data. Event data relates to actions performed by users post-installation, such as in-app purchases, registrations, and level completions. In AppsFlyer, event data is available grouped by the user acquisition date or the event date.
25: Post-install event data grouped by user acquisition date is referred to as lifetime value (LTV).
26: Post-install event data grouped by event date is referred to as activity.
27: Note
28: : Installs are neither LTV nor activity.
29: Advertisers find both types of data useful but for different purposes. For this reason, both are available.
30: LTV data
31: LTV data are the events performed during the lifetime of a user who converted/installed the app in a specific date range. The date range refers to users who installed during the time period and shows how valuable they are during their time as customers. If a user converted/installed the app before the specified date, then even if events occurred during the specified date range, they don't show in LTV dashboards and reports.
32: LTV data is a tool that shows the
33: quality of users
34: from different media sources. Campaign optimization depends on LTV data.
35: Activity data
36: Activity data shows what users did during a specified date range. meaning what events were performed by active app users during a specified date range. It doesn't matter if the users converted/installed the app outside of the date range.
37: Because activity data shows a breakdown of chronological events, it's useful for measuring the overall performance of media sources during specific date ranges. For example, use activity data to see how many purchase events were performed by all app users during a specific month.
38: Use activity data to compare user behavior in the current month relative to a previous month.
39: The train analogy
40: This analogy will help you understand the difference between activity and LTV data.
41: Activity:
42: Imagine you're watching a passing train. As the train passes, you see only the actions performed by the passengers on the train as they pass by. This is activity data.
43: LTV
44: : Now imagine, that you board a train as an observer. The train is divided into railroad cars.
45: You board the car with other passengers at the departure platform. This is the install.
46: During the journey, you're able to observe all the actions performed by the passengers in the car. You observe the actions of these passengers until a passenger deboards the train, this is an uninstall.
47: You aren't able to view the actions of passengers in other railroad cars because they boarded the train before or after you. This then is LTV.
48: AppsFlyer dashboards and reports—LTV or activity?
49: The dashboards enable marketers to optimize their non-organic traffic. Most of the dashboards are LTV-based, as marketers typically measure performance on an LTV basis. All aggregated data reports are LTV-based, and all raw data reports are activity-based.

2: using UnityEngine.Scripting;
3: 
4: namespace Unity.Services.Authentication.PlayerAccounts
5: {
6:     /// <summary>
7:     /// Represents the claims contained within an ID token obtained during sign-in.
8:     /// </summary>
9:     public class IdToken : BaseJwt
10:     {
11:         /// <summary>
12:         /// Constructor
13:         /// </summary>
14:         [Preserve]
15:         internal IdToken() { }
16: 
17:         /// <summary>
18:         /// Gets the audience of the ID token.
19:         /// </summary>
20:         [JsonProperty("aud")]
21:         public string[] Audience;
22: 
23:         /// <summary>
24:         /// Gets the email of the user.
25:         /// </summary>
26:         [JsonProperty("email")]
27:         public string Email { get; set; }
28: 
29:         /// <summary>
30:         /// Indicates whether the user's email address is verified.
31:         /// </summary>
32:         [JsonProperty("email_verified")]
33:         public bool EmailVerified { get; set; }
34: 
35:         /// <summary>
36:         /// Indicates whether the user's email address is private.
37:         /// </summary>
38:         [JsonProperty("is_private_email")]
39:         public bool IsPrivateEmail { get; set; }
40: 
41:         /// <summary>
42:         /// Gets the issuer of the ID token.
43:         /// </summary>
44:         [JsonProperty("iss")]
45:         public string Issuer;
46: 
47:         /// <summary>
48:         /// Gets the JWT ID of the ID token.
49:         /// </summary>
50:         [JsonProperty("jti")]
51:         public string JwtId;
52: 
53:         /// <summary>
54:         /// Gets the nonce value used during the authentication request.
55:         /// </summary>
56:         [JsonProperty("nonce")]
57:         public string Nonce { get; set; }
58: 
59:         /// <summary>
60:         /// Gets the subject identifier of the user.
61:         /// </summary>
62:         [JsonProperty("sub")]
63:         public string Subject;
64:     }
65: }

12: > Use Unity's comprehensive sign-in solution that provides persistent accounts across games, devices, and platforms.
13: 
14: ## Overview
15: 
16: Unity Player Accounts is Unity's comprehensive sign-in solution that supports persistence across games, devices and platforms. It's an end-to-end account system that includes a user flow UX, email and password, social sign-in options, and data access and deletion flows.
17: 
18: Unity Player Accounts is an external identity provider which is natively integrated with Unity Gaming Services and the Authentication SDK. It has multiple benefits such as SSO, organization-level player pool, and cross-game, cross-device or cross-platform gameplay.
19: 
20: | Technical feature                                | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
21: | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
22: | Integrated with Unity Gaming Services and Editor | Player Accounts is the out-of-the-box sign-in and identity solution for Unity Gaming Services and Unity's ecosystem. It's seamlessly integrated with Authentication and offers additional features such as organization-level player identifiers.                                                                                                                     |
23: | Cross-platform and cross-device                  | Your players can sign up and sign into your games across a range of platforms, including iOS, Android, Windows, and macOS.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
24: | Cross-game                                       | Leverage organization-level player identifiers to maintain persistent player profiles across all of your games.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
25: | Streamlined user sign-up & sign-in journey       | Your players can sign up or sign in to their accounts using their preferred method, such as email and password or social accounts like Google or Apple.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
26: | Integrate once and forget it                     | Our browser-based sign-up and sign-in flow is automatically updated with new features without any integration or update for your game. Focus on building and running your game, without the need to reintegrate your authentication solution. Once integrated, you can rely on Player Accounts to stay up to date with the latest security improvements and features. |
27: 
28: ## Get started
29: 
30: To get started you must first [install the Authentication package](./get-started.md), and then configure a Unity Player Accounts ID provider in the Unity Dashboard.
31: 
32: The C# methods required for interacting with Unity Player Accounts are included within the Authentication package in the dedicated `PlayerAccountService` namespace.
33: 
34: ### Set up the Unity Player Accounts ID provider
35: 
36: You can set up Unity Player Accounts directly in the Unity Dashboard.
37: 
38: 1. In the Unity Editor select **Services** > **Authentication** > **Configure** from the navigation menu.
39: 2. Select **Go to Dashboard** to open the Authentication Identity providers web page.
40: 3. On the web page, select **Add Identity Provider** and select **Unity Player Accounts**.
41: 4. Enter the provider details in the **Add Unity Player Accounts** dialog.
42:    > **Note:**
43:    >
44:    > For the sign-in flow to work in the Unity Editor Play mode, include the **PC** platform.
45: 5. Select **Add provider**.
46: 6. Return to **Services** > **Authentication** > **Configure** in the Unity Editor and select **Refresh**. This displays the **Unity Player Accounts** ID provider.
47: 7. In the Unity Editor, navigate to **Services** > **Unity Player Accounts** > **Configure** and ensure the Client ID is correctly set. This is also where you can optionally configure scopes and custom redirect URI schemes.
48: 
49: > **Note:**
50: >
51: > The authentication flow works without the need for configuring the redirect URI, as long as the registered URIs follow the prescribed format:
52: >
53: > * Desktop/Standalone: `http://localhost/callback`
54: > * Android/IOS default deep link URI: `unitydl://com.unityplayeraccounts.{unity-project-id}`
55: 
56: ### Before you publish your game
57: 
58: Review Unity's compliance and branding guidelines:
59: 
60: * You must provide a way for players to request data deletion and disclosure requests for your application and their Unity Player Account.
61: * Include a link to the Unity Player Accounts account deletion page: `https://player-account.unity.com/delete-account`
62: * Include a link to the Unity Player Accounts privacy support email for data disclosure or other privacy requests: `unity-player-login-privacy@unity3d.com`
63: * You must always ensure compliance with [Unity Terms of Service](https://unity.com/legal/terms-of-service).
64: * You must always maintain, display, and abide by a conspicuously placed Privacy Policy that makes appropriate disclosure to end-users, complies with all applicable privacy and data protection laws and regulations, and grants Unity the necessary rights required for the use of the Unity Player Accounts service.
65: 
66: ### Unity Player Accounts sample
67: 
68: The Authentication package includes a sample scene which is fully integrated with Unity Player Accounts. Use this sample to try out the flow after completing the configuration steps above.
69: 
70: To import the sample, follow these steps:
71: 
72: 1. In the Unity Editor, select **Window** > **Package Management**.
73: 2. Select the Authentication package.
74: 3. Select **Samples** > **Import**.
75: 
76: Open the sample scene under **Assets** > **Samples** > **Authentication** > \[Package-Version] > **UI Example** > **UnityPlayerAccountsUIExample**.
77: 
78: ## Sign in a returning player or create new player
79: 
80: Use the `PlayerAccountService.Instance.StartSignInAsync` method to start the player sign-in flow for Unity Player Accounts. This opens the system browser to `https://player-login.unity.com`, prompts the player to sign in, and then returns them to the application with their Unity Player Accounts credentials.
81: 
82: When they have signed in to Unity Player Accounts and returned to your application with their credentials, use the `AuthenticationService.Instance.SignInWithUnityAsync` method to either:
83: 
84: * Create a new Unity Authentication player with the Unity Player Accounts credentials.
85: * Sign in an existing player using the Unity Player Accounts credentials.
86: 
87: The `PlayerAccountService.Instance.SignedIn` event will let us know when the browser-based Unity Player Accounts sign in has succeeded and we can proceed with signing in to Unity Authentication.
88: 
89: The credentials required to sign in to Unity Authentication are the access token available on `PlayerAccountService.Instance.AccessToken`.
90: 
91: ```cs
92: async void Start()
93: {
94:     await UnityServices.InitializeAsync();
95: 
96:     // Register the Unity Player Accounts sign-in event handler after services initialization.
97:     PlayerAccountService.Instance.SignedIn += SignInWithUnityAuth;
98: }
99: 
100: // Call this from a button or other application-specific trigger to begin the sign-in flow.
101: async void StartPlayerAccountsSignInAsync()

10: # Manage linked external identities
11: 
12: > Handle account linking conflicts and manage multiple linked external identities for players.
13: 
14: Managing a player’s linked external identities is important to ensure your players can secure their accounts and use the access method of their choice. When offering account linking to your customers, it's important to properly handle every scenario.
15: 
16: A player can have multiple linked unique external identities (e.g. Apple, Facebook, Google). However, an external identity can only be linked to a single player (e.g. one player ID cannot be linked to multiple Google identities).
17: 
18: ### Retrieve a player's information
19: 
20: `GetPlayerInfoAsync()` can be used to load a player’s information which includes their linked identities.
21: 
22: ### Handle account linking conflicts
23: 
24: The linking operations will throw an error if an identity is already linked to another player.
25: 
26: When there’s a conflict, it’s important to inform the player of the situation.
27: 
28: An optional parameter can be provided to force the link to be created. Using this option will remove the initial link which can make the initial account unrecoverable.
29: 
30: We recommend offering the following options in case of conflict:
31: 
32: * Choose to force the link and keep the current account.
33: * Choose to switch to the initial account by using the `SignInWith*` API.
34: * Choose to cancel the action and remain in the current state.
35: 
36: 
37: **Frame:**
38: ![An example workflow for identity management that presents the previously mentioned options for how to handle conflicts. ](/api/media?file=/authentication/media/images/identity-management.png)

1: On this page
2: UID2 overview
3: Unified ID 2.0 overview
4: UID2 is a framework that enables deterministic identity for advertising opportunities on the open internet for many
5: participants
6: across the advertising ecosystem. The UID2 framework enables publisher websites, mobile apps, and Connected TV (CTV) apps to monetize through programmatic workflows. Built as an open-source, standalone solution with its own unique namespace, the framework offers privacy controls designed to help participants meet local market requirements.
7: note
8: The term "UID2" can refer to either the framework or an actual identifier. Unless otherwise indicated, this page provides an overview of the UID2 framework.
9: Guiding principles
10: ​
11: The UID2 framework has the following principles as its foundation:
12: First-party relationships
13: : UID2 enables advertisers to activate their first-party data on publisher websites across the open internet.
14: Non-proprietary (universal) standard
15: : All
16: participants
17: in the advertising ecosystem who execute an appropriate participation agreement can access UID2.
18: Open source
19: : The source code for the
20: UID2 component services
21: is publicly available.
22: Interoperable
23: : The framework allows other identity solutions (commercial and proprietary) to integrate and provide UID2 tokens with their offerings.
24: Secure and encrypted data
25: : UID2 leverages multiple layers of security to help protect user and other participant data.
26: Consumer control
27: : Consumers can opt out of UID2 at any time through the
28: Transparency and Control Portal
29: .
30: Technical design principles
31: ​
32: The UID2 framework is built on the following technical principles:
33: Distributed integration
34: : Multiple certified integration paths provide options for publishers, advertisers, and third-party data providers to manage and exchange UID2 tokens.
35: Decentralized storage
36: : The framework does not have centralized storage for personal data (
37: DII
38: ) mappings. All participants maintain only their own data.
39: Lean infrastructure
40: : The UID2 system is light and inexpensive to operate.
41: Internet scale
42: : The UID2 infrastructure can scale to address the continuously increasing needs of
43: participants
44: and to meet the performance demands of specific geographic regions.
45: Self-reliant
46: : UID2 does not rely on external services for the processing of real-time bidding (RTB) data.
47: Elements of the UID2 infrastructure
48: ​
49: For information about key elements of the UID2 infrastructure, and other aspects of UID2, refer to the following pages:

6: Track unique users
7: Amplitude counts unique users by combining three identifiers (device ID, user ID, and Amplitude ID) into a single profile across anonymous sessions, sign-ins, and multiple devices. Send a stable user ID as soon as a person authenticates so anonymous events on the same device merge into one profile and your active-user counts stay accurate.
8: How Amplitude identifies unique users
9: The three IDs work like this:
10: Device ID
11: : For mobile applications, Amplitude pulls the Identifier for Vendors,
12: IDFV
13: , or generates a random alphanumeric string for the device ID. For web applications, Amplitude sets the device ID to a randomly generated Universally Unique Identifier,
14: UUID
15: , by default. The device ID persists unless a user clears browser cookies or browses in private mode.
16: User ID
17: : You configure the user ID. Many products use a username or an internal unique identifier as the user ID. Use a stable value for the user ID. Don't assign anonymous users a user ID. Anonymous users still have Amplitude IDs and device IDs, so Amplitude might recognize them as the same user later.
18: Amplitude ID
19: : After Amplitude receives a device ID, a user ID, or both, Amplitude generates the Amplitude ID and associates it with the collected identifiers. Amplitude needs only one identifier to generate an Amplitude ID. Amplitude prefers the user ID because multiple unique users could share the same device.
20: If Amplitude encounters a known device ID that is already tied to a user ID in a different project, Amplitude assumes the device ID is tied to that user ID in all projects, even if you don't have the Portfolio add-on. For more information, refer to
21: Portfolios
22: .
23: When multiple projects reside in a single organization, all projects must use the same variable as the user ID. Using the same user ID variable prevents tracking discrepancies. For example, if one project uses email addresses as user IDs and another project uses phone numbers, Amplitude doesn't merge those identifiers into the same Amplitude user profile. If you're on
24: MTU billing
25: , you might incur charges for multiple users.
26: Use advertising identifiers as the device ID
27: You can configure Amplitude to use the Identifier for Advertiser,
28: IDFA for iOS
29: , and the Advertising Identifier,
30: AdID for Android
31: , as the device ID. For more information, refer to the relevant SDK installation guide. Using advertising identifiers causes the device ID to persist across installs.
32: iOS users can reset the IDFA on their devices at any time. As of iOS 10, if a user limits ad tracking, iOS returns an IDFA of all zeros. Amplitude instead sets the device ID to either the IDFV or a randomly generated string.
33: Android users can reset the AdID on their devices at any time.
34: Set up cross-domain tracking
35: You can track anonymous behavior across two domains. For example:
36: Site 1:
37: https://www.landingpage.com
38: .
39: Site 2:
40: https://www.productpage.com
41: .
42: To track an anonymous user who starts on Site 1 and navigates to Site 2, pass both the device ID and session ID from Site 1 as URL parameters to Site 2. Passing only the device ID preserves anonymous identity but doesn't maintain session continuity. Sessions that split across the domain boundary can distort session-based metrics like traffic source analysis.
43: For Browser SDK 2 (
44: @amplitude/analytics-browser
45: v2.8.0 and later):
46: From Site 1, get the device ID from
47: amplitude.getDeviceId()
48: and the session ID from
49: amplitude.getSessionId()
50: .
51: Pass both values to Site 2 as URL parameters when the user navigates. For example:
52: https://www.productpage.com?ampDeviceId=DEVICE_ID&ampSessionId=SESSION_ID
53: .
54: Initialize the Amplitude SDK on Site 2 with
55: amplitude.init('YOUR_API_KEY')
56: . The SDK reads
57: ampDeviceId
58: and
59: ampSessionId
60: from the URL automatically.
61: A custom time-based session definition can supplement session-based reporting, but it doesn't replace passing
62: ampSessionId
63: for true SDK session continuity across domains. For full implementation details, refer to
64: Cross-domain tracking
65: in the Browser SDK 2 documentation.

33: TargetAd and AdKDD 2017
34: .  As usual when we publish research work on Criteo related data, we publicly release the dataset used for the experiments in the paper.
35: Compared to other online advertising datasets such as CTR prediction dataset or Conversion Modelling datasets, this one contains attribution data, i.e if the conversions are attributed to Criteo or not by the advertisers. This important information opens a new set of applications in the area of real-time bidding and conversion modeling in online advertising.
36: In our paper we show that using a simple attribution model in the bidder can significantly improve bidding performance, providing better ROI for the advertiser and reduced ad exposure for the user,  compared to baseline last-click bidder.
37: Content of this dataset
38: This dataset includes following files:
39: README.md
40: criteo_attribution
41: _
42: dataset.tsv.gz
43: : the dataset itself (623M compressed)
44: Experiments.ipynb
45: : ipython notebook with code and utilities to reproduce the results in the paper. Can also be used as a starting point for further research on this data. It requires python 3.* and standard scientific libraries such as pandas, numpy and sklearn.
46: Data description
47: This dataset represents a sample of 30 days of Criteo live traffic data. Each line corresponds to one impression (a banner) that was displayed to a user. For each banner we have detailed information about the context, if it was clicked, if it led to a conversion and if it led to a conversion that was attributed to Criteo or not. Data has been sub-sampled and anonymized so as not to disclose proprietary elements.
48: Here is a detailed description of the fields (they are tab-separated in the file):
49: timestamp
50: : timestamp of the impression (starting from 0 for the first impression). The dataset is sorted according to timestamp.
51: uid
52: a unique user identifier
53: campaign
54: a unique identifier for the campaign
55: conversion
56: 1 if there was a conversion in the 30 days after the impression (independently of whether this impression was last click or not)
57: conversion_timestamp
58: the timestamp of the conversion or -1 if no conversion was observed
59: conversion_id
60: a unique identifier for each conversion (so that timelines can be reconstructed if needed). -1 if there was no conversion
61: attribution
62: 1 if the conversion was attributed to Criteo, 0 otherwise
63: click
64: 1 if the impression was clicked, 0 otherwise
65: click_pos
66: the position of the click before a conversion (0 for first-click)
67: click_nb
68: number of clicks. More than 1 if there was several clicks before a conversion
69: cost
70: the price paid by Criteo for this display (
71: disclaimer:
72: not the real price, only a transformed version of it)
73: cpo
74: the cost-per-order in case of attributed conversion (
75: disclaimer:
76: not the real price, only a transformed version of it)
77: time_since_last_click
78: the time since the last click (in s) for the given impression

72: Data deduplication is a critical task in data management and mining, focused on consolidating duplicate records that refer to the same entity. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is a critical class of data for deduplication across various industries. Consumer data, stored and generated through various engagement channels, is crucial for marketers, agencies, and publishers. However, a major challenge to PII data deduplication is the lack of open-source benchmark datasets due to stringent privacy concerns, which hinders the research, development, and evaluation of robust solutions.
73: This paper addresses this critical lack of PII deduplication benchmarks by introducing the first open-source, high-quality dataset for this task. We provide two datasets: one with 1,000,000 unlabeled synthetic PII profiles and a subset of 10,000 pairs curated and labeled by trained annotators as matches or non-matches. Our datasets contain synthetic profiles built from publicly available sources that do not represent any real individuals, thus ensuring privacy and ethical compliance. We provide several challenging data variations to evaluate the effectiveness of various deduplication techniques, including traditional supervised methods, deep-learning approaches, and large language models (LLMs). Our work aims to set a new standard for PII deduplication, paving the way for more accurate and secure solutions. We share our data publicly at this link

1: Copy Page
2: About RampID Translation
3: Use the Translation endpoint to translate RampIDs from one partner encoding to another.
4: 📘
5: RampID translation was formerly known as "RampID transcoding". You might continue to see instances of "transcode", "transcoding", and "transcoded" in some places.
6: 🚧
7: Every RampID has a specific encoding to ensure the security and privacy of our partner's data. Due to the sensitive nature of RampIDs, certain privacy restrictions must be validated before translation access is provided. To enable this feature, contact your LiveRamp representative.
8: The API translates RampIDs from one partner encoding to another, enabling each partner to maintain control of their unique RampIDs in a secure collaboration.
9: Calls to translate RampIDs can be made as a single transaction call (for a single RampID) or as a batch request call (to translate up to 1,000 RampIDs per call).  We recommend you use batch requests whenever possible.
10: For more information, see "
11: Identity Translation
12: " in the Identity help.
13: RampID Structure
14: Each RampID consists of three parts:
15: The two-letter prefix, which denotes whether the RampID is maintained  (
16: XY
17: for individuals and
18: HY
19: for households) or derived (
20: Xi
21: or
22: Hi
23: for households)
24: The four-digit partner encoding (sometimes abbreviated to just "encoding"), which uniquely identifies the partner
25: The unique value that identifies the person or household
26: The default encoding for the RampIDs that you receive is called your "native encoding".
27: Other-to-Native Translation
28: When you receive RampIDs in encodings that are different from your default, you translate them to your native encoding.  Each partner encoding you would like to translate from requires an explicit one-time authorization to be performed by our client support team.
29: Once  this authorization is configured, you can send any RampID in any authorized encoding to the API and  then call the
30: /people/anonymousAbilitec/
31: endpoint (for individuals) or the
32: /households/anonymousAbilitec/
33: endpoint (for households) to receive that specific RampID in your native encoding.
34: Native-to-Other Translation
35: 📘
36: The ability to perform native-to-other translation requires proper authorization setup. Your LiveRamp representative will properly permission and provide partner encodings to you.
37: You can translate RampIDs from your native encoding to another entity's encoding by providing the partner encoding directly as a query parameter.
38: Requesting RampID Translation Permissions
39: Translation permissions depend on a two-way agreement between your company and the partner whose RampIDs you wish to translate. This agreement must explicitly consent to the translation while specifying the translation direction (native-to-other or other-to-native).
40: When you contact your LiveRamp representative about obtaining translation permissions, they will email both you and your partner to obtain this consent, cc:ing
41: [email protected]
42: .
43: The email for the partner doing the translation will read:
44: Please confirm permission to translate Company A RampIDs into Company 
45: B RampIDs.  Once received, your permission may be revoked at 
46: any time via email to
47: [email protected]
48: .
49: The email for the partner translated from will read:
50: Please confirm permission to translate Company A RampIDs into Company B RampIDs.  
51:  Once received, your permission may be revoked at any time via email to
52: [email protected]
53: .
54: If you are translating both to and from a partner's RampIDs, you must obtain separate permission for each translation direction:
55: Please confirm permission to translate Company A RampIDs into Company 
56: B RampIDs and to translate Company B RampIDs into 
57: Company A RampIDs.  Once received, your permission may be revoked at any time via 
58: email to
59: [email protected]
